role: Source of bw_old: the benchmark with the old read kernel, run in part A.
purpose: This C program is the benchmark before the change of 2026-11-13: each thread runs one kernel (read, write or copy) over its own buffer for at least a set time, and the program prints the total rate in GB/s. Its function `k_read` is the old read kernel: portable C code with 16 running sums, where each load is followed by an add.

main_flow.step: `main` sets the defaults and reads the arguments. In the whole-chip test ra.sh passes `--threads 120 --cpus 0-119 --bytes 256M --kernel K --reps 3 --min-ms 500`, with one kernel name K per process [Ref3].
`main` checks the arguments. The buffer size must be a multiple of 256 B.
`main` creates a barrier for 121 threads (120 workers plus itself) and starts the 120 worker threads. Thread i gets CPU i.
Each worker pins itself to its CPU, reserves a buffer of 256 MiB and writes every element once (first touch). None of this is timed.
For each of the 3 repetitions, each worker runs one warm-up pass that is not timed and then waits at the barrier.

All workers leave the barrier together. Each worker reads the clock, runs whole passes of the kernel over its buffer, and reads the clock after every pass. It stops after the first pass that ends 0.5 s or more after its start.
For kernel `read`, each pass is one call of `k_read`: 16 running sums, one add per loaded 8-byte element, and one stored sum per pass.
`main` waits until all workers have stopped. It divides the bytes of all threads by the longest thread time and prints one row with this rate (`aggregate_GBps`).
After the last repetition `main` prints a `best` row, waits for the end of the threads and exits.

behavior_notes: What is timed: the passes of the kernel and the clock reads between them (lines 314 to 320). Pinning, buffer allocation, first touch, the warm-up pass and the waits at the barrier are not timed.

Stop rule (whole-pass stop): in the whole-chip test a thread reads the clock after every pass. It stops at the first end of a pass that lies 0.5 s or more after its own start. The threads stop at different times. Between the first stop and the last stop, fewer than 120 threads read memory.

Rate: `aggregate_GBps` = bytes of all threads / longest thread time / 1e9 (GB = 1e9 bytes). It is never above the sum of the thread rates. Example: the first `read` row of bw_old in the result folder k120-T72A1-20261117T221209Z shows 467.83 GB/s. In the same row, 120 times the mean thread rate of 3.99 GB/s is about 479 GB/s [Ref5].

Few passes per interval: in that example row the 120 threads completed 954 passes together, which is 7.95 passes per thread on average. The longest thread time was 0.5474 s [Ref5]. So one pass is about one eighth of the bytes that a thread counts in an interval.

The old read kernel in the machine code of bw_old: one loop pass reads 128 B with 4 `ldp q` loads. It adds the loaded values to 8 vector registers with 8 `add` instructions [Ref1]. Per 256 B this is 8 loads and 16 vector adds, 32 instructions in total. The new read kernel of bw_new has the same 8 loads per 256 B and no vector add, 11 instructions in total [Ref1].
`k_read` is portable C, so the compiler chooses the machine code. The statements about the machine code hold for the binary bw_old only (gcc 14.2.0, flags in [Ref1]).
The sum that `k_read` returns is stored to a `volatile` variable once per pass over the buffer (line 264). This store is the reason why the compiler must keep the loads and the adds.

Kernels that the whole-chip test runs from bw_old: all six (`read`, `write`, `copy`, `asmread`, `asmwrite`, `asmcopy`). ra.sh starts one process per kernel and round, which gives 12 processes of bw_old per call of ra.sh, each with 3 timed intervals [Ref3]. The rerun of 2026-11-17 has 3 result folders of part A with 12 processes of bw_old each [Ref5]. The comparison of the old with the new read kernel uses the kernel `read` of both binaries [Ref6].

The six kernels in bw_old and in bw_new: the machine code of the three C kernels `k_read`, `k_write` and `k_copy` differs between the two binaries. The three asm kernels (`k_asmread`, `k_asmwrite` and `k_asmcopy`, written as assembly text) have the same instructions in both binaries, at other addresses [Ref1]. So a comparison of bw_old with bw_new for `write` or `copy` also compares different code. For an asm kernel it compares the same instructions of the kernel.

Code around the kernels in the old and the new source: the new source is the file bandwidth.c of the same folder. The command `diff` on the two files shows every difference [Ref8]. In the new source the old `k_read`, `k_write` and `k_copy` (lines 138 to 160) and the old `pass` (lines 260 to 286) are text inside comments, and new versions of these four functions follow them. The comments of lines 135 to 137 and 257 to 259 are replaced. The variable `sink` (line 292) is removed, and the calls of `pass` in lines 312 and 318 have no `&sink`. One include line is new, and line 335 of the usage text differs. No other line of this file differs in the new source. So `now_s`, `pin_cpu`, `alloc_buf`, the three asm kernels, the clock reads and the stop rule of `worker`, and the whole function `main` with the rate computation are the same source text in both files. This is a statement about the source text. For bw_old and bw_new the objdump text of the build shows the six kernels only [Ref1].

Which text of bandwidth.c was compared: the local file [Ref8]. Its sha256 is the value that the build of 18:32:18 UTC on 2026-11-13 recorded for bandwidth.c [Ref9]. The build of 18:12:22 UTC recorded another sha256 for bandwidth.c [Ref1]. The timed runs of 2026-11-13 followed that build. Both builds recorded the same sha256 for bw_new, and ra.sh runs bw_new only with this sha256 [Ref1] [Ref9] [Ref3]. So the machine code of bw_new is not in doubt. The two texts differ in comment lines only. An edit of 2026-11-13 18:32:07 UTC replaced 2 comment lines above `k_read` with the 5 comment lines 178 to 182 of the local text [Ref10]. With this edit reversed, the local text has the sha256 value of the earlier text (c1406e02...). No code line differs. None exists under the folder cache-perf.

Order inside a process: buffer write (first touch), then for each repetition one warm-up pass and one timed interval. The code has no sleep between them: a thread only waits at the barrier for the other threads. ra.sh selects one kernel per process, so no kernel is timed after another kernel in the same process [Ref3].

Build: run_kernels.sh built bw_old on 2026-11-13 with gcc 14.2.0 and the flags `-O3 -march=native -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns -pthread -Wall -Wextra -std=gnu11` [Ref1] [Ref2]. ra.sh builds nothing. It checks the sha256 of bw_old and stops when the value differs [Ref3]. The value that ra.sh expects is the value that the build recorded for bw_old [Ref1]. Each of the 3 calls of ra.sh in the rerun recorded the same value for bw_old [Ref7]. So the objdump text of that build shows the machine code of bw_old that ran in part A. The binary bw_old is not in the local folders. Its sha256 value is known only from these records. The sha256 of this source file, computed on 2026-11-21, equals the value that the build recorded [Ref1].

2 MiB pages: the program asks for them with `madvise` and never checks the result. The header line of each process prints `thp=madvise`. This text shows the request only. The Linux setting for transparent huge pages was `always` at the start of each of the 3 calls of ra.sh [Ref7]. With `always`, Linux may use 2 MiB pages for a buffer without a request. Insufficient data: whether the buffers of part A lay on 2 MiB pages. A run of the same kernel with bwx12 would record it. bwx12 prints rows of the kind P, and a P row holds the page state of one buffer [Ref6].
Main thread: the program does not pin it. ra.sh runs under `taskset -c 0-119`, so the main thread may run on any of the CPUs 0 to 119 [Ref3]. It waits at the barrier during every timed interval.

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the whole-chip read test of 2026-11-17, run after the memory speed was lowered from 8000 MT/s to 7200 MT/s.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
million transfers per second, the unit of memory speed.
one of the six inner loops of this benchmark: read, write, copy, asmread, asmwrite, asmcopy. It never means the Linux kernel.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12. In this file it is the function `k_read`.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.

a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers. In this file it is the function `k_asmread`.
the new read kernel or asmread.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source. This file, bandwidth.orig.c, is the old source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.
one start of a benchmark binary.
one timed measurement inside a process. The code calls it a repetition (`rep`). The option `--reps 3` gives 3 intervals per kernel.
in part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
a pass is one call of a kernel. It goes once over the whole buffer of a thread. A loop pass is one execution of the loop body inside a kernel (128 B in `k_read`, 256 B in the asm kernels).
the stop rule of bandwidth.c: after the minimum time (0.5 s here) each thread finishes the pass over its buffer that it is in. The threads stop at different times.
one pass that a thread runs before each timed interval. It is not timed.
GB = 1e9 bytes. MiB = 2^20 bytes (1048576 bytes). 256 MiB = 268435456 bytes.
bind a thread to one CPU. Linux then runs the thread only on that CPU.
the first write to the pages of a new buffer. Linux assigns the physical memory at that moment.
memory pages of 2 MiB, larger than the base pages of Linux. The option name `--no-thp` uses the Linux name "transparent huge pages" (THP).
an object of the POSIX thread library. A thread that calls `pthread_barrier_wait` waits until a set number of threads have called it. Then all of them continue together.
the 128-bit vector instructions of Arm. A NEON register (`v0` to `v31`, written `q0` to `q31` when all 16 bytes are used) holds for example two 64-bit integers.
Scalable Vector Extension, a second set of vector instructions of Arm. The processor fixes its vector length.
`ldp q` is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers (32 B). `stp q` is the Arm instruction that stores two 16-byte vector registers (32 B).
the instruction set of CRB. The asm kernels exist only in a build for it.
the script of part A. It starts bw_old and bw_new with 120 threads, one process per kernel, binary and round.
the script of 2026-11-13. It built bw_old and bw_new and wrote the machine code of their kernels to the file probe.txt.
the machine code of a binary, printed as assembly text by the tool objdump.

code in the machine code of `k_read` of bw_old that is not in the source. At the start of the function it copies a guard value to the stack. Before the return it compares the copy with the guard value. If the two differ, it calls `__stack_chk_fail`.
the GNU C compiler. run_kernels.sh built bw_old and bw_new with its version 14.2.0.
a Linux command. It starts a program that may run only on the CPUs of the given list.
a command that prints the lines in which two text files differ.
analysis scripts of the rerun. They read the interval rows that this program prints.
a checksum. Two files with the same sha256 have the same content.
the number that a process returns when it ends. 0 means success.

functions.name: now_s
functions.what: Reads the monotonic clock of Linux and returns seconds.

functions.name: parse_bytes
functions.what: Turns a size text such as 256M into bytes.

functions.name: parse_cpus
functions.what: Turns a CPU list such as 0-119 into the entries of cfg.cpus.

functions.name: pin_cpu
functions.what: Pins the calling thread to one CPU.

functions.name: alloc_buf
functions.what: Reserves one buffer on a 2 MiB boundary and asks Linux for 2 MiB pages.

functions.name: k_read
functions.what: The old read kernel: adds every 8-byte element of the buffer to one of 16 sums and returns the total.

functions.name: k_write
functions.what: C write kernel: stores one value into every element. Also used, not timed, for the first touch.

functions.name: k_copy
functions.what: C copy kernel: copies every element from one buffer to the other.

functions.name: k_asmread
functions.what: Hand-written load-only loop: 8 ldp q loads per 256 B, loaded values not used.

functions.name: k_asmwrite
functions.what: Hand-written store-only loop: 8 stp q stores per 256 B.

functions.name: k_asmcopy
functions.what: Hand-written copy loop: 8 ldp q loads, then 8 stp q stores per 256 B.

functions.name: pass
functions.what: Runs the selected kernel once over the buffer of a thread and returns the bytes to count.

functions.name: worker
functions.what: One thread: pins itself, writes its buffer, then per repetition runs a warm-up pass and times whole passes.

functions.name: usage
functions.what: Prints the list of options and ends the program with exit status 2.

functions.name: main
functions.what: Reads the arguments, starts the threads, and prints one rate row per timed interval.
